In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple says it is still waiting for leaker Jon Prosser to provide additional documents and is hoping to re-depose Michael Ramacciotti, with both defendants pushing back against Apple's handling of the case. Details below.

According to a joint status report submitted to Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who is to blame for the delays in the trade secrets lawsuit, which Apple filed against both defendants in July 2025.

A bit of background

Reminder: shortly after unveiling iOS 26, Apple sued Prosser and Ramacciotti over a Prosser video that leaked a number of aspects of the OS, including what turned out to be the final confirmation of the Liquid Glass visual overhaul.

Apple alleged that Ramacciotti had improperly accessed a developer's iPhone belonging to an Apple employee who was later fired; Ramacciotti then FaceTimed Prosser to show him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

The case has produced plenty of drama since, including a default being entered against Prosser for failing to timely respond to Apple's complaint (though Prosser has pushed back against the characterization that he was ignoring the case, declining to comment).

Eight months later, a court agreed to vacate that default and give him another chance to formally answer the lawsuit.

Ramacciotti, for his part, has responded to Apple's complaint and largely complied with Apple's document production requests, court filings show.

But things have shifted since Prosser hired a lawyer and formally entered the case, with all three sides increasingly squabbling over who is responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosures and the resulting delays.

The new joint status report

Turning back to that new status report, Apple says it wants Ramacciotti to update his responses to written interrogatories and be re-deposed to address what it calls "the inconsistencies between his deposition and Mr. Prosser's."

Ramacciotti says he's willing to be deposed again, provided Apple provides "a roadmap for resolution of the claims against him, including whether Apple still needs additional discovery from him (if any)."

As for Prosser, Apple says it's "still waiting on certain additional documents requested over three months ago, including revenue reports and analytics for his YouTube channel, as well as related communications with third parties that he referenced during his deposition."

Prosser, for his part, argues: "It appears that the trade secrets at issue are no longer trade secrets and have entered the public domain." In other words, his argument seems to be that because Apple has now shipped its Liquid Glass iOS update, the very information at the heart of the lawsuit is public and therefore no longer qualifies as secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti is asking the court to hold a status hearing this month, at which Apple would be required to spell out what additional discovery it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to then have 30 days to either voluntarily drop its claims against him or commit to pushing the case toward trial.

For its part, Apple wants to press on with discovery, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti, and to obtain the still-outstanding Prosser documents. Prosser argues he's already met the document production obligations he agreed to and pushes back against Apple's continuing requests for more.

If Judge Donato doesn't grant Ramacciotti's request for a status hearing, the parties have suggested filing another joint status report on December 2.
